slides.name: 1 · How does AI actually 'think'?

params.text: Understanding the technology behind the tools you use

slides.notes:
AI AWARENESS DAY 2026 · Starter 2 · Principle: SMART · 5 minutes

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
· Understand that AI predicts patterns rather than "thinking"
· Recognise the difference between pattern prediction and understanding
· Learn why AI 'hallucinations' occur

THE ONE THING TO WATCH FOR — from the teacher pack:
Students will anthropomorphise AI. Gently correct "it thinks" to "it predicts", every time, all the way through. That single substitution is most of the learning.

Avoid being dismissive of AI's usefulness while explaining its limits.

slides.name: 2 · Statement · frame

params.text: When you ask ChatGPT a question, do you think it 'understands' you the way a human would?
Talk to the person next to you — 60 seconds

slides.notes:
The vote is the hook. Take it before you say anything, and leave the result on screen while you work through the next slide — you want the room looking at their own answer as the explanation arrives.

"Somewhere in between" is the most popular answer in most rooms and it is the most interesting one to unpick: what would "partly understand" even mean?

DISCUSSION PROMPTS
→ What is the difference between knowing something and predicting it?
→ Why might it matter if AI does not truly understand?
→ How might knowing this change how you use AI tools?

slides.name: 3 · Predicting is not understanding
slides.notes:
This slide is the whole starter. If you only have two minutes, show the question and then this.

The analogy that lands best, from the teacher pack: AI is a very sophisticated autocomplete, not a thinking being.

Row 3 is the one students find most surprising — a model has no mechanism for noticing that it does not know, which is exactly why hallucinations sound as confident as facts.

slides.name: 4 · It predicts the next word — and it is wrong often enough to matter

params.text: It predicts the next word — and it is wrong often enough to matter
UK university students using AI for academic work — HEPI Survey 2025
Students naming hallucinations as a major concern — HEPI Survey 2025
School students who have used AI — HEPI 2025

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: Trained on billions of web pages, books and articles · HEPI 2025, MIT, Stanford AI Index 2025

slides.notes:
The point of putting 92% next to 51% is that both are true at once: nearly everyone is using it, and half of them already know it makes things up. The room is not naive — it is under-equipped.

A hallucination is not a rare glitch. It is what the prediction mechanism does when the pattern runs out.

slides.name: 5 · So — does it understand you?

params.text: AI processes text as mathematical patterns, not meaning.
It works out which words are likely to come next, from its training data.
No feelings, no memories, no consciousness to draw on.
Coherent and fluent and completely incorrect, all at once.

slides.notes:
Reveal one at a time.

Do not skip the last card. The teacher pack is explicit about this: explaining the limits should not tip into dismissing the tool. Students who conclude "AI is rubbish" have missed the lesson as thoroughly as students who conclude "AI knows everything".

LAB — SlideForge shows 6 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: Understanding needs more — Context, common sense and real-world knowledge that AI lacks.; But it is still useful — A powerful tool when you know what it is doing..

slides.name: 6 · Statement · frame

params.text: Does it matter if AI doesn't understand, as long as it's helpful?
Extension — if you have longer than five minutes

slides.notes:
HIDDEN BY DEFAULT — the teacher pack's sub-question. Unhide with the card slide after it.

A scale rather than a poll: this is a question of degree, and the spread across the room is more interesting than any single answer. The distribution usually splits, which is the discussion.

slides.name: 7 · Yes — it matters

params.text: No understanding means hallucinations are built in, not a bug.
Plausible-sounding wrong advice on health, legal or safety questions.
Without understanding, it can't know when it's wrong.
Verify outputs rather than trusting them.

slides.notes:
Extension — unhide together with the question before it.

LAB — SlideForge shows 5 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: Knowing the limits helps — You use a tool better when you know what it cannot do..

slides.name: 8 · Two words worth knowing

params.text: AI trained on billions of texts to predict and generate human-like language, by pattern rather than by meaning.
When AI confidently generates false information — because it predicts 'likely' text, not verified facts.

slides.notes:
Both definitions were in the teacher pack only. Worth writing down.

"Hallucination" is an unfortunate term — it implies a mind having a strange experience. If a student notices that, they have understood the lesson better than the industry that named it.

slides.name: 9 · Being AI-smart

params.text: Five habits that follow from knowing how it works
A pattern-matching tool, not a thinking being — it doesn't 'know' facts.
Always check AI outputs against reliable sources — don't trust it blindly.
It reflects patterns in its training data, including biases and errors.
Knowing HOW AI works helps you use it more effectively.
The more specific your question, the better the output.

slides.notes: Reveal one at a time. If you are short of time, end here.

params.text: AI is a powerful tool — but like any tool, it has to be used properly.

slides.name: 11 · Section · If any of this affected you

params.text: If any of this affected you
You will not be in trouble for asking for help.

slides.notes:
Say this out loud rather than leaving it on the slide.

Your tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead is available to help — name the actual person if you can.

From the teacher pack, the three messages that matter most:
· If you are targeted by deepfake abuse, it is NOT your fault.
· Creating AI-generated intimate images of anyone is illegal.
· You will NOT be in trouble for reporting — we are here to help.

Have the safeguarding details ready to share privately with anyone who comes to you afterwards.
